reference.source: Rook's Textbook of Dermatology / WHO Classification of Skin Tumours
clinicalPearls: A benign tumour of follicular (hair-germ) differentiation, presenting as skin-coloured firm papules or nodules
The multiple familial form clusters symmetrically on the central face, especially the nasolabial folds, nose, and forehead, appearing around puberty
Multiple familial trichoepithelioma is linked to CYLD mutations and overlaps with Brooke-Spiegler syndrome and familial cylindromatosis
The chief diagnostic challenge is distinguishing it histologically from basal cell carcinoma, which it closely mimics
Helpful discriminators favouring trichoepithelioma include papillary mesenchymal bodies, a fibrocytic stroma, absence of a peritumoural cleft, and stromal amyloid
Immunohistochemistry, for example CD10 stromal versus tumoural patterns and other markers, can aid the distinction from basal cell carcinoma in difficult cases
Solitary lesions are usually excised, while multiple facial lesions are managed for cosmetic reasons and tend to recur
reference.pathophysiology: Trichoepithelioma is a benign adnexal neoplasm derived from hair-germ (follicular) epithelium. It is composed of basaloid cells arranged in nests and cords with follicular differentiation, characteristically forming keratin-filled horn cysts and papillary mesenchymal bodies within a cellular fibrocytic stroma. The multiple familial variant arises from germline loss-of-function mutations in the CYLD tumour-suppressor gene, the same gene underlying cylindromas and spiradenomas, so it forms part of the CYLD-related spectrum with Brooke-Spiegler syndrome; loss of CYLD deregulates nuclear factor-kappa B signalling and promotes follicular tumour formation. Although architecturally and cytologically it resembles basal cell carcinoma, it lacks the aggressive infiltrative and destructive behaviour of that malignancy.
additionalDifferentials: Basal cell carcinoma (especially the keratotic and infiltrative types)
Desmoplastic trichoepithelioma versus microcystic adnexal carcinoma
Angiofibromas (as in tuberous sclerosis) for facial papules
additionalInvestigations: Skin examination noting central-facial symmetry and multiplicity
Skin biopsy with histopathology showing horn cysts and papillary mesenchymal bodies
Immunohistochemistry (for example CD10 and other markers) to distinguish from basal cell carcinoma
Family history and examination for cylindromas and spiradenomas
CYLD genetic testing when multiple familial trichoepithelioma or Brooke-Spiegler syndrome is suspected
redFlags: A solitary lesion enlarging, ulcerating, or behaving aggressively, raising concern for basal cell carcinoma
New infiltrative or destructive change in a previously stable lesion
Family clustering of adnexal tumours indicating a hereditary CYLD syndrome
reference.prognosis: Trichoepitheliomas are benign with an excellent prognosis; solitary lesions are cured by excision, whereas multiple familial lesions persist and recur and cause cosmetic morbidity. Malignant transformation is rare.
pitfalls: Overdiagnosing basal cell carcinoma on a superficial or partial biopsy and pursuing unnecessary aggressive treatment
Conversely, dismissing a genuine basal cell carcinoma as a trichoepithelioma
Missing the hereditary CYLD context in patients with multiple facial lesions
Confusing desmoplastic trichoepithelioma with microcystic adnexal carcinoma on limited tissue
management: Manage a solitary lesion by complete surgical excision, which is curative and provides histology to confirm the diagnosis
For multiple familial lesions, use ablative or destructive techniques such as carbon dioxide laser, electrosurgery or dermabrasion to reduce cosmetic burden, accepting that lesions tend to recur
Maintain histological vigilance with biopsy of atypical or changing lesions to distinguish from and detect basal cell carcinoma and the rare malignant transformation
Offer CYLD genetic testing and counselling, and screen relatives and the patient for cylindromas and spiradenomas within the Brooke-Spiegler spectrum
Provide psychological support and reassurance for the cosmetic morbidity of extensive central-facial disease
Follow up through dermatology and dermatopathology, with plastic surgery input for reconstruction where lesions are numerous or disfiguring
